scenarios.title: The Social Media Break
scenarios.text: You take a month off social media after a rough stretch, the apps deleted and the password changed. On day three you keep reaching for a phone that has nothing on it.

choices.label: Stay off the whole month
choices.result: The whole month, off. By week three you stop reaching for your phone, and you read two books and sleep better than in years.

choices.label: Have someone post for you
choices.result: Someone else posts the basics for you: game days, charity events. You don't read the replies, and it's the perfect middle.

choices.label: Spend the time with people
choices.result: The time, spent with real people instead: long dinners, a walk with {best_friend}, an afternoon with {parent}. It's so much better.

scenarios.title: The Charity Ride
scenarios.text: You ride in a charity bike ride across the state with four teammates: three hundred miles, five days, and a support van driven by the equipment manager.

choices.label: Ride with the slowest group
choices.result: The slowest group, the whole way, telling stories. You finish last, laughing, and the charity raises the most it ever has.

choices.label: Ride it hard
choices.result: Hard, every day, at the front. Your legs hate you by day three, and the charity gets a huge photo of you at the finish line.

choices.label: Organize the team's riders
choices.result: The team's riders and the support van, organized by you. Everyone finishes, nobody gets lost, and the equipment manager calls you 'boss'.

scenarios.title: The Coach Who Believed in You
scenarios.text: The coach who gave you your first chance is in the hospital after a heart attack. He's seventy-three, and his wife says he keeps asking about your last game.

choices.label: Visit on your day off
choices.result: A day off, spent at his bedside. He's thin and pale and still giving you notes about your follow-through, which makes you laugh.

choices.label: Call his family
choices.result: His family, called, to ask what would actually help. You do all of it, including fixing his porch steps yourself on a Sunday.

choices.label: Send a long letter
choices.result: A long letter, handwritten over two nights, about everything he did for you. His wife reads it to him, twice, and he keeps it.

scenarios.title: The Teammate's Kid
scenarios.text: A teammate's ten-year-old wants to kick and asks you for lessons, very formally, in a handwritten letter he delivers to your locker himself, wearing a tie.

choices.label: Teach him every Saturday
choices.result: Saturday mornings, all fall, on the practice field. He's good, and so is his smile, and his father watches from the fence every week.

choices.label: Make it a family thing
choices.result: Your family and his, together every Saturday: kicking first, then pancakes. The two families become very close over the season.

choices.label: Give one lesson and cleats
choices.result: One proper lesson and a pair of cleats, signed. He wears the cleats to bed for a month and to school for another.

scenarios.title: The Prime-Time Interview
scenarios.text: A national network wants an in-depth interview about your whole career: two days of filming, your hometown, your family, the hard years. It will air before the playoffs.

choices.label: Open up about the hard years
choices.result: The hard years, told honestly on camera. People write to you for weeks, and some of the letters make you cry.

choices.label: Prepare carefully
choices.result: Every answer, prepared and true, rehearsed twice with {best_friend}. It's a strong piece, and you say exactly what you mean on camera.

choices.label: Keep it light
choices.result: Light and funny, nothing heavy at all. It's a nice piece about nothing much, and {parent} likes it best of everything.

scenarios.title: The Neighbor's Kid
scenarios.text: The neighbor's kid practices kicking in the street every day after school, against a recycling bin, with a ball that's lost most of its air.

choices.label: Show him one thing
choices.result: One thing, shown from the curb: the plant foot. He does it right the next day, and waves at your window.

choices.label: Set up a net in your driveway
choices.result: A net in your driveway, with a new ball, and a sign that says it's his. His mother brings you cookies.

choices.label: Watch from the window
choices.result: From your kitchen window, every afternoon, you watch him kick against the recycling bin and remember, exactly, what it was like being that kid.

scenarios.title: Running the Music
scenarios.text: You've been the locker room DJ for six years, and a rookie wants the job. He has a speaker the size of a refrigerator and opinions about your playlists.

choices.label: Hand it over with a speech
choices.result: The aux cord, handed over with a ceremony and a speech about responsibility. The room cheers, and he plays your favorite song first.

choices.label: Share the job
choices.result: Fridays are his, the rest are yours. It works, and his Fridays are better than you would ever admit out loud.

choices.label: Make him earn it
choices.result: A month of proving himself, playlist by playlist. His is better, and you admit it in front of the whole team meeting.

scenarios.title: The Contract Year Pressure at Home
scenarios.text: Contract year again, and the conversations at home are getting shorter. {love_interest} has stopped asking how practice went, and you've stopped offering anything at all.

choices.label: Talk about all of it
choices.result: All of it, one night after the kids are asleep: the fear, the money, the next city. It's long and hard and the best talk in months.

choices.label: Plan for every outcome
choices.result: A plan for every outcome, written down together: stay, move, retire. It helps, because nothing will be a surprise anymore.

choices.label: Focus on kicking
choices.result: Kicking, only kicking, and home gets quieter. The contract comes in March, and the quiet takes much longer to fix.

scenarios.title: The Halfway Point
scenarios.text: A reporter asks if you think you're halfway through your career. You're thirty-two, it's a fair question, and you have no idea how to answer it.

choices.label: Give a careful answer
choices.result: Focused on this season, you say, which is true. Later, in the car, you think about the question for a long time.

choices.label: Joke about it
choices.result: You hope it's a third, you say, and the room laughs. The clip goes around, and {parent} sends it to everyone he knows.

choices.label: Say you're just starting
choices.result: Just getting started, you say, and you mean it. The column the next day calls you 'defiant', which you like.

scenarios.title: The Club's Ring of Honor Nominee
scenarios.text: Fans start a petition to nominate you for the club's ring of honor while you're still playing. It has forty thousand signatures, and the owner has seen it.

choices.label: Thank the fans
choices.result: Thanks, online and in person at the next home game. The fans cheer loudly, and the petition hits sixty thousand by Monday.

choices.label: Ask them to wait
choices.result: Wait until you're done, you ask the fans kindly. They agree, and it gives everyone something to look forward to.

choices.label: Keep it to yourself
choices.result: A smile, kept to yourself, and back to practice. It means more than you'd ever say out loud, even to {parent}.

scenarios.title: The Middle-Aged Rookie
scenarios.text: A thirty-year-old rookie kicker joins the club after years of tryouts, day jobs and empty stadiums at midnight. Everyone keeps saying you two should talk.

choices.label: Talk to him
choices.result: You talk to him over lunch. He spent six years kicking at midnight in a high school stadium, and you leave the table humbled.

choices.label: Help him
choices.result: You help him learn the league: travel, routines, which coaches mean what. He's grateful and fast, which makes you nervous.

choices.label: Stay focused
choices.result: Polite, and focused on your job. He's still competition, whatever his story is, and his story won't keep your job for you.

scenarios.title: The Retirement Seminar
scenarios.text: The union holds a retirement seminar on a Tuesday night. You sit in the back row, near the door, in case you want to leave.

choices.label: Take notes
choices.result: Notes, pages of them, in the back row. Some of it scares you, usefully, and you call your advisor on the drive home.

choices.label: Bring a teammate
choices.result: You bring a teammate who needs it more than you do. He doesn't say a word all night and asks for your notes the next day.

choices.label: Leave early
choices.result: You leave at the break. Not yet. In the parking lot, you sit in the car a while before you start it.

scenarios.title: The Family Photo
scenarios.text: The family photo for the team's holiday card, in matching sweaters, and nobody is smiling: the baby is crying, the dog is escaping, and your eldest is furious about the sweater.

choices.label: Make them laugh
choices.result: A ridiculous face, and everyone laughs at once. The photo is chaos and perfect, and the club uses it on the cover.

choices.label: Bribe with dessert
choices.result: Dessert, promised loudly to everyone. They all smile on cue, the photographer thanks you, and the dog stays put for once.

choices.label: Go with the grumpy one
choices.result: The grumpy photo, kept on purpose. It becomes the family's favorite picture of all time, framed in the hallway forever.
